newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-U.S. transport sector wary as fuel costs dip.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-U.S. transport sector wary as fuel costs dip.

text.p: A recent slide in fuel costs has helped ease the pressure on the U.S transportation sector after a year in which prices surged to their highest since the end of the Gulf War.
But many in the industry remain wary that the trend may prove only temporary, particularly if this winter turns out colder than usual.
"With normal weather everything will be alright. But if we have a cold winter, all bets are off," said an executive in charge of fuel buying at a major U.S. airline.

"We're looking forward to a downward correction," said David Swierenga, chief economist at the Air Transport Association in Washington, D.C. "But we're hoping that everyone who may be paying those high prices for home heating oil will fly south for the winter."
U.S. truckers and airline operators have joined their counterparts around the world in recent weeks in slapping on fuel surcharges in order to make up for some of the increased overhead.
British Airways led the pack with a 2.5 percent charge on European routes from mid-October, followed by other European and American airlines as well as trucking and other shippers.
Jet and diesel prices in the key New York market may be down between 12 and 14 percent in the last month, but those surcharges are likely to stick, industry sources said.

"The good news on prices is only relative," said Kenneth Simonson, chief economist at the Washington D.C.-based American Trucking Associations (ATA). "If you go back 12 months (retail) prices were about 20 percent lower than they are now," Simonson said.

Indeed, wholesale prices of New York jet fuel during 1994 and 1995 were remarkably stable, ranging about five cents either side of 50 cents a gallon during the period. This year, prices have averaged just above 63 cents a gallon and have soared as high as 85.90 cents a gallon, a post-Gulf War high set in the spring.
This much higher volatility has meant that fuel retailers are more reluctant to pass on any dip in prices, reflected in the still sticky retail diesel prices paid by truckers.

According to U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) data, the average U.S. retail price for on-road diesel remains at about $1.32 a gallon, hardly down from a month ago and well higher than the $1.12 a gallon at this time last year.

Transportation is one of the most fuel-intensive industries, with the trucking industry spending up to 20 percent of revenue on it, according to Simonson of the Trucking Associations. Each five percent increase in fuel costs translates into a one percent rise for truckers' customers, assuming it is passed on, he said.
For the airline industry, jet fuel accounts for between 10 and 15 percent of total operating costs.

American Airlines chairman Robert Crandall said on Monday that the airline's fuel costs so far this year have risen by between $300 million and $400 million, adding that "for every one cent rise in fuel prices, our bill rises by $30 million a year."
American Airlines said last Friday that it was adding a 10 cents-a-kg cargo fuel surcharge on most international routes from November 15.

Meanwhile, U.S. rail fuel costs have risen by about 12 percent over the year, though with fuel amounting to about seven percent of overall costs the effect on the sector is felt less, according to industry officials.
